stature.source: typical: the drafter's figure for trees on canyon walls and ledges below the rim; tall: Wikipedia citing Flora of North America, to 9 m; record: FEIS, 3-12 m; read 2026-11-10

roots.note: roots gripping the rock at the foot of a ledge or a sandstone wall

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a small, crooked tree or tall shrub of two to several stems from a short base, round-topped, with brownish-grey scaly bark and dark green, birch-like toothed leaves; pale hop-like fruit clusters hanging in summer, yellow leaves in fall

description: A small, crooked tree or tall shrub, usually a few metres high, whose short trunk splits into several slender, twisting stems under a rounded crown. The bark is brownish grey and breaks into small loose scales, the leaves are oval, sharply toothed and birch-like, and in summer it hangs with pale clusters of papery sacs like hops, each holding a small nut. At the Grand Canyon it is rare and local, growing on the canyon walls and ledges just below the rims.

season_notes.winter: Bare grey-brown crooked stems against the canyon rock; small male catkins wait at the twig tips.
season_notes.spring: Slender male catkins hang and shed pollen in March to May, before or as the leaves open.
season_notes.summer: Dark green leaves; pale green hop-like fruit clusters hang from the twigs and dry to tan.
season_notes.fall: Leaves turn yellow; the papery fruit clusters drift off on the wind with their nuts.

range.where: the canyon walls, ledges and the foot of cliffs just below the South Rim of the Grand Canyon, local and sporadic; Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas, in oak and pinyon-juniper woodland and the lower ponderosa pine zone

notes: The library has no Ostrya or Carpinus; downy birch (the template, a card on white alder) is the same family (Betulaceae) with a small multi-stemmed tree shape and oval, toothed, birch-like leaves (Wikipedia, Ostrya: leaves doubly toothed, resembling birch), and its hanging catkins stand for the hop-like fruit clusters. The card replaces the birch's white bark with brownish-grey scaly bark (FEIS: shallowly furrowed, breaking into loose small scales 2.5-5 cm; Wikipedia: brownish grey, furrowed into scales or strips), hence shreddy, and its streamside roots with roots on rock (the drafter's). Height 3-12 m (FEIS), to 9 m (Wikipedia citing Flora of North America); the brief draws it in the shrub layer, so 2.5-7 m; USDA PLANTS lists shrub and tree. Form: a short trunk splitting into several slender crooked branches, round-topped (FEIS, Wikipedia); the 2-6 stems are the drafter's reading of that. Leaves 2.5-6.3 cm (FEIS), leaf_size_m 0.045. Male catkins 1.3-3.2 cm, March-May, before or with the leaves (FEIS); the fruit is a nutlet about 6 mm (FEIS) in a bladder-like involucre, in pendulous clusters 3-8 cm (Wikipedia, Ostrya), so the catkins are drawn pale, 5 cm (the drafter's). Habitat: oak woodland, pinyon-juniper and the lower ponderosa pine zone, sunny, dry, well-drained sites in mountains and canyons, at the bases of sandstone monoliths (FEIS), sunny and dry (Wikipedia); Wikipedia names the rims of the Grand Canyon; the canyon-wall placing is from the brief. The north and shade values above 1 and 0.4 are the drafter's, for a tree of canyon walls; FEIS says shade tolerance is undocumented. Elevation commonly 1280-2130 m (FEIS); the South Rim at about 2100 m is near the top of that. Fire: probably top-killed or killed by most fires, recolonising from wind-borne seed (FEIS), hence disturbed 0.4. Eaters: neither FEIS nor Wikipedia records any browse, seed or cover use (FEIS mentions only breeding birds in canyonland habitats); mule deer browse and the deer mouse and dark-eyed junco as cover are the drafter's guesses for a small canyon tree and should be checked. NPS Grand Canyon pages (trees, shrubs, natural features) were read and do not name this species. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, leaf-on months and the fruit clusters' colour and size are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
